title: Real-Time Scheduling
summary: Scheduling for deadlines, not fairness — Rate Monotonic and Earliest Deadline First, worked with real numbers and a schedulability test.

slides.markdown:
Everything so far in this group optimizes for average-case goals — low waiting time, fairness, throughput. Real-time scheduling optimizes for a completely different thing: **meeting every deadline**, where being fast on average is worthless if even one deadline is missed.

This topic covers the two classic real-time algorithms — Rate Monotonic (fixed priority) and Earliest Deadline First (dynamic priority) — with a worked numeric example showing exactly how to test whether a set of periodic tasks can even be scheduled at all.

slides.sectionTitle: Real-time scheduling goals: meeting deadlines, not just fairness
slides.markdown:
Every scheduler in this group so far cares about *how well* jobs do on average — minimize waiting time, be fair, keep the CPU busy. Real-time scheduling asks a binary question instead: does every task complete before its deadline, every single time? A task that finishes 1% late isn't "slightly worse," it's a **failure**, full stop.

Most real-time systems deal with **periodic tasks**: a task with period `T` must run once every `T` time units, needing `C` units of CPU time each period (its worst-case execution time), forever, for as long as the system runs. An anti-lock braking system's wheel-speed sensor read might need `C=1ms` of CPU every `T=10ms`, indefinitely.

The scheduling question becomes: given several such periodic tasks sharing one CPU, is there *any* valid schedule where all of them always meet their deadlines? This topic's tools (RM, EDF, and the schedulability test) exist to answer that question, ideally before the system ever ships.

slides.sectionTitle: Hard real-time vs soft real-time systems
slides.markdown:
This distinction (introduced briefly in [What Is an Operating System](what-is-an-operating-system)) determines how much engineering rigor a missed deadline demands.

| | Hard real-time | Soft real-time |
|---|---|---|
| Missed deadline means | Total system failure — potentially catastrophic | Degraded quality, still "working" |
| Example | Airbag deployment, pacemaker, anti-lock brakes | Video streaming, online gaming |
| Design approach | Provable worst-case guarantees, formal schedulability analysis | Statistical/average-case tuning, occasional misses tolerated |
| Typical scheduler | RM or EDF with a formal admission test | General-purpose OS scheduler, sometimes with real-time priority classes |

**How to decide which a system needs:** ask what happens on the very first missed deadline — if the honest answer is "someone could be hurt" or "the system is unsafe," it's hard real-time and needs the rigor of this topic's formal tools, not just "make it fast."

slides.sectionTitle: Rate Monotonic Scheduling: fixed priority by period
slides.markdown:
**Rate Monotonic (RM)** scheduling assigns each periodic task a fixed priority based purely on its period: shorter period means higher priority, permanently, for the task's entire lifetime — a task that must run every 5ms always outranks one that runs every 50ms, regardless of anything else.

The intuition: a task with a short period has less slack — it comes around again soon, so delaying it risks its very next deadline quickly. A long-period task has more breathing room before its next deadline, so it can afford to wait behind more urgent, tighter-period work.

RM is provably optimal among *fixed-priority* algorithms — no other fixed-priority assignment can schedule a task set that RM cannot — but that optimality claim is scoped specifically to fixed priority, not to real-time scheduling in general (EDF, with dynamic priority, can do strictly better, as the comparison slide shows).

slides.sectionTitle: Earliest Deadline First: dynamic priority by deadline
slides.markdown:
**Earliest Deadline First (EDF)** recalculates priority dynamically: at every scheduling decision, run whichever ready task's *absolute next deadline* is soonest — a task's priority isn't fixed to its period, it changes constantly as deadlines approach and pass.

This is strictly more powerful than RM: EDF is provably optimal among *all* possible scheduling algorithms for meeting deadlines on a single processor — if any schedule exists that meets every deadline for a task set, EDF will find one. RM can fail to schedule task sets that EDF handles successfully, precisely because RM's fixed priority can't adapt when a normally-lower-priority task's deadline suddenly becomes the most urgent one.

The cost of that extra power is implementation complexity and overhead: EDF needs to recompute and compare deadlines continuously (more bookkeeping per scheduling decision) versus RM's simple, unchanging priority lookup — a real engineering trade-off between optimality and implementation simplicity/predictability.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: RM vs EDF schedule for the same task set
slides.markdown:
![Rate Monotonic vs EDF Gantt chart](assets/rm-vs-edf-gantt.svg)

This specific task set (A: period 4, exec 2; B: period 6, exec 3) is a textbook example where RM's fixed-priority rule genuinely fails to meet all deadlines, while EDF, given the identical total CPU demand, succeeds — a concrete demonstration that RM's optimality claim really is scoped to "best among fixed-priority," not "best overall."

Total utilization here is 2/4 + 3/6 = 0.5 + 0.5 = 1.0 — fully saturating the CPU, which is exactly the boundary condition where RM's more conservative bound and EDF's tighter bound (next slide) diverge in practice.

slides.sectionTitle: Schedulability tests — can this task set meet its deadlines?
slides.markdown:
For EDF, the test is simple and exact: a task set is schedulable if and only if total CPU utilization `U = Σ(Cᵢ/Tᵢ)` is at most 1.0 (100%) — EDF can always find a valid schedule up to full utilization, no safety margin needed.

For RM, the classic Liu & Layland bound is more conservative: a task set of `n` tasks is *guaranteed* schedulable if `U ≤ n(2^(1/n) − 1)`, which converges to about 69.3% as `n` grows large.

```
Task set: Task A (period 20ms, exec 5ms), Task B (period 50ms, exec 15ms)
Utilization: U = 5/20 + 15/50 = 0.25 + 0.30 = 0.55

RM bound for n=2: 2(2^(1/2) - 1) ≈ 2(1.414 - 1) ≈ 0.828

Since U (0.55) <= 0.828, this task set is guaranteed schedulable under RM.
It's also comfortably under EDF's 1.0 bound, so both algorithms would work here.
```

Note the RM bound is *sufficient but not necessary* — a task set can pass above the bound and still happen to be schedulable in a specific case, but below the bound it's guaranteed safe regardless of specifics, which is what makes it usable for pre-deployment worst-case verification.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: assuming a general-purpose scheduler can give real-time guarantees
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "If I just raise this task's priority to maximum on Linux/Windows, it'll behave like a real-time system."

**Why it's wrong:** raising priority changes *relative* ordering among ready tasks, but a general-purpose scheduler makes no formal guarantee about worst-case latency at all — no schedulability analysis, no bounded interrupt-handling delay, no protection from priority inversion by default, and critically, the kernel itself can still delay a "high priority" user task arbitrarily long inside its own non-preemptible sections (some kernel code paths, certain driver operations) with no accounting for real-time deadlines whatsoever.

**Correct model:** genuine hard real-time guarantees require a scheduler (and often a whole kernel — an RTOS, or a real-time-patched kernel like Linux's `PREEMPT_RT`) explicitly designed to bound worst-case latency everywhere, not just at the scheduler's priority-comparison step — a task's nominal priority is only one factor among many that determine its actual worst-case delay.

slides.sectionTitle: Senior nuance: priority inversion and priority inheritance
slides.markdown:
A staff-level real-time hazard beyond basic scheduling: **priority inversion** occurs when a high-priority task is blocked waiting for a lock held by a low-priority task, and a *medium*-priority task (unrelated to the lock) preempts the low-priority task in between — the high-priority task ends up waiting on the medium-priority task indirectly, even though the medium task has nothing to do with the resource it actually needs.

This isn't theoretical: it famously caused watchdog-triggered resets on the 1997 Mars Pathfinder mission, traced to exactly this pattern in its VxWorks RTOS, and fixed remotely via a software patch enabling **priority inheritance** — a fix where a low-priority task holding a needed lock is temporarily boosted to the priority of the highest task waiting on it, so no unrelated medium-priority task can cut in during the wait.

This is a favorite senior-level interview topic specifically because it combines two ideas (scheduling priority and mutual exclusion) that seem unrelated until this exact failure mode connects them — and it comes with a genuinely famous, citable real-world incident.

slides.sectionTitle: How this shows up in production
slides.markdown:
Linux exposes real-time scheduling policies directly: `SCHED_FIFO` and `SCHED_RR` implement fixed-priority scheduling (RM-adjacent) for user processes that request it via `sched_setscheduler()`, letting audio production software, industrial control interfaces, or robotics stacks opt into bounded-latency behavior on an otherwise general-purpose kernel — though without `PREEMPT_RT` patches, worst-case guarantees remain looser than a dedicated RTOS.

Message brokers and trading systems that promise strict latency SLAs ("process this message within 1ms, 99.99% of the time") are solving a soft-real-time-flavored version of this exact problem — and teams building them do run utilization-style calculations (how much guaranteed capacity does each message class need) conceptually similar to the RM/EDF schedulability test, even without calling it that.

When debugging a real-time or latency-critical system that occasionally misses its deadline under load, checking for priority inversion (a high-priority task blocked behind a lock held by something unexpectedly low-priority) is a genuinely common root cause worth checking early, not a rare edge case.

slides.sectionTitle: Beyond the basics: when deadline isn't the same as period
slides.markdown:
Both RM and EDF as described assume a task's deadline equals its period — it must finish exactly before it needs to run again. Real systems often need a task to finish *sooner* than that: a sensor reading might need processing within 2ms even though it's only sampled every 10ms, leaving 8ms of intentional slack for other work.

**Deadline Monotonic (DM)** scheduling generalizes RM for exactly this case: instead of prioritizing by period, it prioritizes by *relative deadline* (shorter deadline = higher priority), which reduces to identical behavior as RM whenever deadline equals period, but produces different — and correct — priority assignments when it doesn't.

The interview-relevant takeaway: if you're ever given a real-time problem where "deadline" and "period" aren't stated as equal, that's a deliberate signal the interviewer wants you to reach for Deadline Monotonic (or EDF, which handles this case natively without any modification) rather than plain Rate Monotonic.
